## Data sources {#sec-data}

We pool vocabulary assessments of children with Down syndrome from several international studies, harmonised onto the common 810-item reference inventory described under [Measures](#measures). Each study contributes parent-report checklist counts of words *understood* and *spoken* — and, for the signing sub-set, words *signed* — together with the child's age in months. The table below inventories each study: the number of observations and distinct children, the age range, and the mean, median and quartiles of each measure (full detail in the accompanying CSV). The figures that follow plot the raw observations, one colour per study.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ds-datasets
#| echo: false
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

_p = Path("figures/descriptives/dataset_summary_ds.csv")
_ds_summary = (
    pd.read_csv(_p)
    if _p.exists()
    else pd.DataFrame({"note": ["Run scripts/generate_descriptive_report.py"]})
)
_ds_summary
```

## Measures

The models report vocabulary counts on a common **810-item reference scale** ($N_{\text{trials}} = 810$). The reference inventory is the DSE vocabulary checklists: Checklists 1, 2 and 3 list 120, 340 and 350 words respectively, so the full set is $120 + 340 + 350 = 810$ words. This is a reference-inventory scale rather than the native denominator for every source checklist: some source forms have lower ceilings, including Wordbank Words & Gestures (396 items), the Oxford CDI (416 items) and the MacArthur-Bates Words & Sentences form (680 items). The common scale keeps estimates comparable across DS and TD instruments, but it remains a modelling approximation, so source-form ceilings and near-ceiling observations should be checked when interpreting high-count regions.

Each source's native checklist ceiling is recorded in the data as `survey_vocab_max`; rows whose count exceeds their form's ceiling are dropped as impossible (data-entry errors) by the form-ceiling guard, but the likelihoods otherwise do not use it: every count is modelled against the common 810-item denominator regardless of the form it came from. A count near a small form's ceiling is therefore effectively right-censored under the harmonisation — a child who checks every item on Words & Gestures (396 items) records 396, which the model treats as one of 810 possible words. The by-source/form counts of at-ceiling and near-ceiling observations are tabulated by `scripts/data_coverage.py` (`ceiling_by_form.csv`) so this exposure can be quantified. In the current data build the exposure is concentrated in the small-ceiling comprehension studies — the Oxford CDI (416-item) source and the MacArthur-Bates Words & Gestures (396-item) source — where about a fifth of comprehension counts fall within 90% of the native ceiling; most other source-and-outcome combinations have none. A dual-form crosswalk shows this harmonisation does not materially bias the estimates, and that the fixed-810 denominator is the right choice rather than a per-form one. The source CDIs are *nested*: the shorter forms comprise the earlier-acquired, more common words, and the items absent from a short form are the rarer words an ability-matched child is unlikely to know — so a short-form count entered against the 810-item denominator is close to the child's true full-inventory fraction, not a length-scaled deflation of it. The uk_02 study administered both the 810-item DSE checklist and the 416-item Oxford CDI to the same children; among those measured on both *at the same age* the median DSE-to-Oxford count ratio for words understood is 1.14, and a Bayesian equating model fitted to all 34 dual-form children (`scripts/crosswalk_dse_oxford.py`) puts the age-adjusted ratio near 1 at the ages where the short forms are actually administered, rising only mildly by school age. Fixed-810 implies a ratio of 1; a per-form denominator ($n_{\text{trials}} = \texttt{survey\_vocab\_max}$) implies $810 / 416 = 1.95$, which the crosswalk excludes across the whole range ($P(R < 1.95) = 1.00$). The fixed 810 denominator is therefore retained as a *validated* approximation, not a documented guess: a per-form rescaling would over-correct badly. The residual is a small, level-dependent undercount for short-form studies — near zero at the young ages where those forms are used, growing only at older ages where almost no short-form data exist — which the study-level random intercepts (VG07 onward) absorb as a level offset, leaving a mild effect only in the non-hierarchical baselines (VG01, VG02, VG05, VG14).

Wordbank Words & Sentences (WS) records are treated as **production-only** because the WS comprehension field is a production proxy rather than an independent comprehension measurement. TD spoken-only models can use WS production counts, but TD bivariate models that estimate both understood and spoken vocabulary exclude WS rows and rely on WG and Oxford CDI observations for the comprehension-production gap.

The us_01 Edgin Down syndrome Wordbank subset carries a further inclusion rule: rows are kept only where production is at most 100 words (`US_01_MAX_PRODUCTION`), a legacy cap retained pending review of its rationale. In the 2026-07 export this excludes 8 of 87 Words & Gestures rows and 24 of 109 Words & Sentences rows from that subset.
